sections.html:
Adverse possession lets a person claim ownership of land they have openly used, against the true owner's wishes, for long enough. It is a doctrine that allows someone to gain a property right in land owned by another, and people sometimes call it squatters' rights.

The plain definition is enjoyment of real property with a claim of right, opposed to another person's claim, that is continuous, exclusive, hostile, open and notorious. The idea is to reward productive use of land and to punish owners who sleep on their rights.

Typical examples are steady use of a private road or driveway and farming an unused parcel. Those look very different from a stranger walking into a vacant house, a difference the rest of this guide returns to.

sections.h2: How long a claimant must possess the land
sections.html:
Twenty years. Under G.L. c. 260, section 21, an action to recover land must be brought within twenty years after the right of action or entry first accrued, or within twenty years after the claimant or those they claim under were seized or possessed of the premises.

Related sections matter too. Section 22 deals with time spent by a predecessor, which counts toward the period, and section 28 deals with open possession. If you inherited a house, ask what happened on the land in earlier owners' time, not only during your own.

The Appeals Court case 1148 Davol Street LLC v. Mechanic's Mill One LLC, 86 Mass. App. Ct. 748 (2014), added that a claim against a private party can begin to accrue while the land was still publicly owned. Time can run in the background longer than owners expect.

Section 21 itself contains one exception: it does not bar an action by or on behalf of a nonprofit land conservation corporation or trust for land held for conservation, parks, recreation, water protection or wildlife protection.

sections.h2: What a squatter has to prove
sections.html:
The claimant carries the burden and must prove every element. Holmes v. Johnson, 324 Mass. 450 (1949), says the burden of proof extends to all the necessary elements of such possession.

Older and newer cases word the elements in similar ways. Cook v. Babcock (1853) calls for actual, open, exclusive and adverse possession and says failure to establish any one is fatal. Ryan v. Stavros, 348 Mass. 251 (1964), puts it as nonpermissive use that is actual, open, notorious, exclusive and adverse for twenty years.

  • Open and notorious: visible enough that a reasonable owner would notice.
  • Exclusive: not shared with the owner or the public.
  • Hostile or nonpermissive: without the owner's permission. Use you allowed in writing or by word is a weak foundation for a claim.
  • Continuous for the full period.

Miller v. Abramson, 95 Mass. App. Ct. 828 (2019), shows that ordinary care can be enough. In that suburban dispute over a sliver of land, mowing and maintaining it as an average owner would supported a finding of adverse possession.

sections.h2: Land that cannot be taken by adverse possession
sections.html:
Registered land, land held by the Commonwealth, and railroad property cannot be taken this way. Three statutes say so.

Land typeStatute
Registered land (Land Court Certificate of Title)G.L. c. 185, section 53
Land held by the CommonwealthG.L. c. 7C, section 32
Railroad propertyG.L. c. 160, section 88

Owners most often benefit from the registered land rule. Section 53 of chapter 185 says no title to registered land, or easement or other right in it against the registered owner, may be gained by prescription or adverse possession, and no right of way by necessity is implied in a conveyance of registered land. If your deed history shows a Certificate of Title, that protection applies.

Whether your parcel is registered or recorded is a title question your attorney or the registry can answer in a few minutes.

sections.h2: Is a squatter the same as an adverse possessor?
sections.html:
No. A person who walks into a vacant house is a trespasser, not someone building a twenty year claim. Adverse possession is not the same as trespassing, and trespass has its own statute.

That statute is G.L. c. 266, section 120. It punishes someone who, without right, enters or remains in a dwelling house, building or improved or enclosed land of another after being forbidden by the person with lawful control, whether directly or by posted notice. The penalty is a fine of up to $100, or up to thirty days in jail, or both. A police officer, sheriff, deputy sheriff or constable may arrest a person found trespassing and hold them up to twenty four hours, Sunday excepted, until a complaint can be made.

The statute has a significant limit. It does not apply to tenants or occupants of residential premises who rightfully entered at the start of a tenancy or occupancy and stay after it has ended or is alleged to have ended. For those people the owner or landlord may recover possession only through appropriate civil proceedings.

sections.h2: What to do about an unauthorized occupant
sections.html:
Document the situation, give a clear written notice that the person is not allowed to stay, and get advice before acting yourself. The right route depends on how the person got in, which is exactly the line section 120 draws between trespassers and people who entered with permission.

  • Someone who never had permission: forbid entry in writing or by posted notice, then involve the police under the trespass statute.
  • Someone who entered as a tenant or occupant and stayed: do not change locks or remove belongings. The statute says possession may be recovered only through civil proceedings.
  • A boundary or use dispute with a neighbor: that is a title question, and a quiet title action in the Land Court is one way owners address it.

Keep dated photographs, copies of any lease or message exchange, and utility records. They show who was in the house and under what terms, and a buyer's attorney will ask for them.

sections.h2: How an occupant claim affects selling
sections.html:
An open dispute over who has the right to occupy or own the land complicates a conventional sale, because a buyer's lender and title attorney need clear title and, usually, possession at closing. That is general closing practice rather than a statute, and your own attorney should confirm what applies to your property.

Deeds to recorded land are filed with the registry of deeds, and under G.L. c. 183, section 4, a conveyance is not valid against most third parties unless recorded. A claim based on long possession is a question about facts on the ground, so ask your attorney how it would show up in a title review.

If you own a house with an unresolved occupant, you can describe the situation to Cash Home Buyers and see whether an as-is purchase fits. An attorney should look at the legal side before any papers are signed.

faqs.q: Can a squatter take ownership of my Massachusetts house?
faqs.a: Only by meeting every element for the full twenty years. G.L. c. 260, section 21 sets the period, and the claimant must prove actual, open, notorious, exclusive and adverse possession without permission. A short stay does not qualify.

faqs.q: How many years does adverse possession take in Massachusetts?
faqs.a: Twenty years under G.L. c. 260, section 21. Time spent by a predecessor in possession can count toward that period under section 22.

faqs.q: Can adverse possession happen on registered land?
faqs.a: No. G.L. c. 185, section 53 says no title to registered land can be acquired by prescription or adverse possession.

faqs.q: Can I remove a squatter myself?
faqs.a: If the person is a trespasser who never had permission, the police can act under G.L. c. 266, section 120. If the person entered as a tenant or occupant, the same section says possession can be recovered only through civil proceedings, so do not use self help.

faqs.q: Is trespassing a crime in Massachusetts?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 120 sets a fine up to $100, up to thirty days in jail, or both, once a person is forbidden to be on the property and stays or returns.
